HEADLINE: Bosilkovski excited to reunite with Connaghan
TEXT:
Incoming Y&R Australia and New Zealand chief executive Pete Bosilkovski has long counted WPP AUNZ chief executive Mike Connaghan as a friend.

During Mr Bosilkovski's stint at WPP's J Walter Thompson between 2000 and 2009 as an account director, Mr Connaghan was managing director from 2004 to 2006.

"I was one of those entrepreneurial guys who always restless, always wanting to make a mark, always wanting to think about how do you go outside the boundaries of what the company stands for and does and then how do you provide innovation for you, for your clients' businesses, and he recognised that," Mr Bosilkovski told The Australian Financial Review.

Mr Connaghan left JWT to become chief executive of STW Group, which had a shareholding in JWT and in 2016 would merge with WPP's local operations. But the move was a loss for Mr Bosilkovski, who would leave the business for Leo Burnett in 2009 and who counted his boss as a mentor.

Mr Bosilkovski at Leo Burnett in Sydney and Mr Connaghan at WPP remained a stone's throw from each other, with both offices in the historic Rocks neighbourhood in Sydney.

"We'd go out because he was only across the road. We'd grab a bite to eat, but we'd walk. It was more about just learning what he's doing with his company, and staying in touch with what I'm doing. After a while it was like 'why be competitors when we can join forces?"' Mr Bosilkovski said.

When the opportunity arose to reunite with Mr Connaghan and take a role with more responsibility, Mr Bosilkovski jumped.

"When I turned up at JWT, he was young and raw, but a real goer, and really passionate about his clients and the business," Mr Connaghan said.

"I'd always said to Pete that one day you will come back. Go and spread your wings and do what you do, but when you do start to think about what you're going to do next, speak to me."

Mr Bosilkovski said it was never a question of if he'd work with his friend again, it was a question of when.

"I worked with Mike 10 years ago at JWT and I always knew we'd work together again. When you work in big multinational corporations you either fall in line and wait for others to pave the way or you can be the change," he said.

"My ethos has always been to never to be the passenger, always stay restless and break new ground. I learnt a lot from Mike. One of the things I learnt early on, is to never accept the word 'can't'. He embraced and injected oxygen in my entrepreneurial way of doing things and it's the reason why I've never lost touch with him."

Mr Bosilkovski said he was excited to run Y&R and take advantage of the global advertising giant's suite of companies to innovate for clients.

"As I look towards Y&R, I can't wait to leverage the power of what Mike has built at WPP and transform Y&R into the creative company of the future. I have a massive passion and obsession for consumer-first brand and business transformation, and joining WPP, which has over 80 diverse companies, I am like a kid in a candy store," he said.

"The opportunity to leverage the very best companies in the world, from tech, data, consumer research, digital, media, PR, design, brand identity etc is very appealing. At Leo Burnett I really enjoyed my time transforming the company from an advertising agency to a creative solutions company, specifically building a future-facing model called Connect and an Innovation Lab called The Diner. And now I'm incredibly excited to build the next chapter and transform Y&R into the future."

HEADLINE: Nine and Ten in the crease for TV rights
TEXT:
Nine Entertainment and Network Ten may lob a joint bid for Cricket Australia's next broadcast rights contract and have spoken to Fox Sports about how pay television can be involved.

There is expected to be plenty of horse-trading before and after today's close of business deadline for bids. Sources say a finalised contract can take time.

Bids for the latest cricket deal are due by 5pm today and all three broadcasters are keen to secure the sport, but they are also reluctant to see sports rights inflating at unsustainable rates.

Sources say Nine, Ten and Fox Sports have held talks regarding how cricket can be shared across the two free-to-air broadcasters and the subscription TV channel, which make sense for their businesses while giving the sport what it needs.

It's believed a three-way joint bid has been explored and may happen, but it is more likely Nine and Ten bid together and, if Fox Sports becomes a part of the deal, it will be after today. Nine and Fox Sports, which is owned by News Corporation, have held ongoing talks regarding a joint bid, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review in February.

The dilemma will be how much cricket goes exclusively behind Foxtel's paywall. Fox Sports will need a certain amount of matches to itself so it can move the dial with subscribers and justify any significant expenditure, while Nine and Ten will be keen to keep as much cricket as they can on their channels and keep costs reined in.

A joint bid from Nine and Ten is expected to be worth between $130 million and $150 million annually. The cost may be further split with Fox Sports' involvement.

Seven West Media is looking at a bid, but sources say it is more to make sure its competitors don't get cricket for a steal, and it is more focused on renewing its Tennis Australia deal.

The free-to-air players need to balance having cricket and the amount of advertising and cross-promotion they can run, while Fox Sports needs to believe cricket can shore up its summer schedule, keep and add subscriptions over the season, as well as book advertising.

Outside revenue, audience reach from free-to-air TV is a crucial pillar for sport, while Cricket Australia will also be tempted by the exposure a mooted dedicated cricket channel from Fox Sports can provide.

As revealed by the Financial Review last week, Cricket Australia's tender documents, sent to potential bidders in early March, pave the way for Fox Sports to play a meaningful role in the carve-up of its broadcast rights.

Cricket Australia is looking for a six-year deal and is said to want at least $150 million annually, or $900 million over the life of the contract, for all the rights.

Cricket Australia has not carved out digital streaming rights as a separate part of its package. All broadcasters, free and pay, will likely demand digital rights as part of any deal.

The last Cricket Australia deal was worth about $500 million in cash and contra over five years.

Key pointsNine and Ten could bid together Monday and Fox Sports join in later.

A joint bid from Nine and

Ten is expected to be worth

between $130m and $150m.

HEADLINE: PlayersVoice raises $4m to go global
TEXT:
Sports athlete media company PlayersVoice has raised an estimated $4 million from investors including technology entrepreneur and Financial Review Young Rich list member Matt Berriman and tennis star Nick Krygios.

The Series A round will fund an overseas expansion for PlayersVoice, which launched last September as an athlete direct publishing platform, and comes as the company clinches a content share deal with News Corporation's Fox Sports.

Other investors in the raising include Pact Group director Lyndsey Cattermole, a former Foster's Group and Tatts Group board member, and existing shareholders.

The business had already attracted investors and board members such as former Young Rich list member Mark Britt, the chief executive of Asian streaming business iFlix, former Saatchi & Saatchi Sydney CEO Simone Bartley and ex-Football Federation Australia media consultant David Mason.

PlayersVoice CEO Kerry McCabe would not reveal the exact amount raised but said the group would use the new funds to expand into the United Kingdom, New Zealand and South Africa, after a successful six months during which internet viewership numbers and engagement exceeded initial expectations.

"Athlete-generated media is the fastest growing category in sports media globally, with this latest round of investment serving to cement our clear market leadership position. It also allows us to build upon a foundation of industry trust and content that has resonated with consumers."

The new funds will also enable PlayersVoice, which features written columns, video posts and podcasts by athletes directly, to roll out more podcast and video content.

Fox Sports and PlayersVoice have also struck an agreement for PlayersVoice content to appear across Fox Sports' suite of broadcast and digital products and channels. "Fans are hungry to learn more and hear from their favourite athletes and this is what PlayersVoice has unearthed," Fox Sports chief operating officer Peter Campbell said.

PlayersVoice claims it has posted content from more than 230 athletes since September and attracted an on-platform audience of more than 1.8 million users that skew significantly younger and more female than many other digital sporting properties. It said the average time a users has read a story is more than six minutes.

Mr McCabe said PlayersVoice faced intense competition in Australia and overseas - the best known athlete content platform is probably the US-based Players Tribune, part-owned by former New York Yankees star Derek Jeter - but was confident his business would emerge as one of the bigger players.

"Like any emerging category there will be winners and losers. I think those who will flourish will solve a market problem and have the ability to scale from a base of business principles."

Athlete-generated media is the fastest growing category in sports media globally. Kerry McCabe, PlayersVoice CEO

HEADLINE: TV sector must accelerate its makeover in the attention economy
TEXT:
If the banks can do it, so too can Australian broadcasters.

Australia's financial system is all-in on an imminent customer payments service from BPay, called Osko, which will easily and instantly allow customers to send and receive money with a simple "PayID", eradicating the need for BSB and account numbers to transact.

BPay and initiatives such as Osko are pointers to what Australia's television networks must do with profound urgency to prosper in the new attention economy. Interestingly, for broadcasters, BPay is equally owned by ANZ, Commonwealth Bank, Westpac and NAB.

The fierce competitive instincts that have delighted many television observers for decades will no doubt continue but those instincts can no longer impede collaboration between all TV networks to reduce complexity and improve the efficacy in trading, audience, data and measurement systems. Silicon Valley's Big Tech operatives in Google, Facebook and Amazon have ensured that.

Their rapacious appetite to raid and decimate local market media economics around the world with global scale and tech smarts is unprecedented. Google and Facebook between them extracted circa $4 billion out of the $13 billion Australian advertising sector last year, according to Morgan Stanley. And the trend is continuing.

Like the banking system's Osko initiative, the first and most urgent step for the broadcast industry is to ensure the trading of more than $4 billion in commercial television airtime each year is faster, easier and ultimately enriched with data intelligence for our customers - advertisers and media agencies. And they too must progress.

Every Australian TV network has now launched its own proprietary system to automate parts of the TV supply chain, from booking and scheduling to predictive audience systems and more refined audience segmentation. But already the advertising market's response to this technology-led innovation is simply one of "more complexity". Advertisers and media agencies today must juggle between three or four competing trading and audience platforms in varying degrees of sophistication through the broadcast system to reach their customers and prospects.

As Peter Horgan, Omnicom Media Group's CEO and chairman of the Media Federation of Australia, said sharply last week, the "transactional headwinds are killing television. It needs to be easier and cleaner to transact. TV is a complicated business but to create three or four complex infrastructures will be wasteful and slow. The boat will be missed."

I agree entirely. It can't work and won't work the way it is but there is real progress being made among Australian broadcasters on alignment. This message came through clearly from advertisers and media agencies at a recent Future of TV Advertising industry forum in which I gave a keynote outlining a five-point action plan the TV sector needed to move on now. One of those points was that broadcasters needed to remove transactional barriers to buying TV and do it fast.

Equally, however, advertisers and media agencies need to embrace the broadcast industry's genuine intent to align on eliminating inefficiencies in the TV system. Those legacy shackles are often as deeply embedded with advertisers and agencies as they are broadcasters. Advertisers such as Westpac's head of media, Toby Dewar, are pointing the way. In an interview with MCN after the Future of TV Advertising forum, Dewar was optimistic about what he was hearing from the broadcast sector at large: "I'm deeply invested in TV succeeding to grow my brand and sales and what's been really encouraging to see is the unity the TV networks have at the moment. I thought there would be more division and history would suggest the networks have all pursued their own path for success. So I'm really encouraged with the sense of collaboration. That focus on pulling it all together, removing the confusion and having one point of entry is quite a profound thing."

To be clear, this promising new era of collaboration by broadcasters must simplify the complexity of buying TV and retain competitiveness. That is all possible. And only once those transactional impediments for TV are addressed, quickly, can we start working on the broader action points broadcasters need to address to keep television local and thriving. Time, however, is not on our side. We must move fast.

Anthony Fitzgerald is chief executive of Multi Channel Network.

HEADLINE: Optus set to sign Euros for 2020
TEXT:
Optus is close to securing local rights to the UEFA Euro 2020 to bolster its sport offering, and the telecommunications provider is expected to compete for the upcoming contract for the Champions League.

The Singtel-owned telco in the box seat to wrap up a deal with the Union of European Football Associations and is likely to beat out incumbent rights holder beIN Sports Australia, which is owned by the Qatari Al Jazeera.

Sources said the deal has not been finalised, but it is more than likely to be wrapped up in the next fortnight.

Optus declined to comment.

A Euros deal would be the latest football competition to be added to Optus' growing suite of content.

In 2015, Optus swooped on rights to the world's most popular domestic football competition, the English Premier League, beating incumbent Fox Sports and beIN Sports. It also has rights to the 2018 FIFA men's World Cup and the 2019 women's World Cup, thanks to a deal signed with SBS in 2016.

Sources said Optus to keen to keep building itself up as a "home for international football" property.

The telco had a record in postpaid handset growth in its last quarter as it built up its EPL offering in its second season - the three-year deal will wrap up in 2019 and Optus are said to be keen to lock the competition down again.

Postpaid handset customers grew by 127,000 in the latest quarter, which was slightly offset by a 29,000 subscriber decline in the less profitable prepaid segment.

Optus could face competition from Fox Sports, which is eyeing off the rights. Bids are due by the end of April for the English Premier League. However, the sports subscription channel is, at this stage, focused on trying to become at part of Cricket Australia's next broadcast rights deal.

Optus had been keen on expanding its cricket rights and had discussions with Cricket Australia. It was particularly keen on the Big Bash League, but has recently cooled on the idea and is more focused on football.

HEADLINE: Nine and Ten may call on Fox Sports in bid for cricket rights
TEXT:
Nine Entertainment and Network Ten will continue to work with Cricket Australia on a bid for its next broadcast deal and are open to bringing in Fox Sports, paving the way for a three-way agreement.

Cricket Australia rejected a joint-bid from Nine and Ten on Friday, as reported by Fairfax Media, but sources said it did not ask the pair for a new offer, rather it just stated their offer was not compliant with requirements outlined in its tender.

In the middle of its negotiations with broadcasters for its next rights deal, Cricket Australia has been rocked by a cheating scandal involving the men's team in South Africa.

Broadcasters were given less than two weeks to submit their bids after the tender was released to interested parties.

Sources said Nine and Ten had previously acknowledged - in order for Cricket Australia to achieve the at least $150 million annual fee it was looking for - that Fox Sports would need to play a role, but the two free-to-air broadcasters and the subscription sports channel had not been able to reach an agreement by the time bids were due at 5pm last Monday.

Cricket Australia's tender outlined 11 different broadcast packages.

"CA can confirm it rejected the bid of the consortium," a Cricket Australia spokesman said. "Discussions are ongoing with other parties."

Fox Sports executives were said to be frustrated by the combined Nine-Ten bid and restrictions imposed by the anti-siphoning list - which dictated the sports free-to-air broadcasters had first rights to bid on - has locked them out of cricket rights negotiations.

As part of Nine and Ten's bid for the rights to Cricket Australia's next six-year contract, the two free-to-air broadcasters promised a greater emphasis on women's cricket, including paying for the production of the women's international Test matches, one-day internationals, Twenty20 internationals and Big Bash League, the costs of which were previously mostly borne by the sporting body.

Industry sources reckoned the production costs of women's cricket would likely be about the $5 million a year mark.

Sources said the bid would see Nine and Ten put an increased emphasis on women's cricket, giving it equal importance to the men's game.

The women's game was a source of tension between Cricket Australia and Nine last year, when the free-to-air network opted not to broadcast the women's Ashes day-night Test match. Instead, Cricket Australia live-streamed the game.

But earlier on in the women's Ashes series, Nine moved the third one-day match from its digital channel Gem to its primary channel.

Sources said Nine would air all women's international cricket under a new deal.

Ten aired 12 women's BBL matches in the 2017-18 summer and it was understood the CBS-owned broadcaster would lift that amount of 23 games from the second year of a new cricket deal, the 2019-2020 summer, when the women's BBL tournament would begin in October rather than December.

Sources said other bids also placed greater interest in the women's game. Fox Sports, Nine and Ten declined to comment.

Australian Test captain Steve Smith admitted he and his leadership team came up with a plan to tamper with the ball during the third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town on Saturday night.

Cricket Australia chief executive James Sutherland hosted a media conference yesterday and announced head of integrity Iain Roy and Pat Howard would fly to South Africa to investigate the cheating incident. No players were yet stood down.

It is unknown what, if any, impact the incident will have of Cricket Australia's broadcast deal negotiations. Broadcasters may use the incident, and ensuing public outcry, as a point to argue down to value of the broadcast rights.

Key pointsThe bid from Nine and Ten promised a greater emphasis on women's cricket.

Broadcasters may use the ball tampering to argue down to value of the rights.

HEADLINE: It's time to finally admit the truth Facebook, it's you, not us
TEXT:
Widespread outrage at the latest scandal to hit social media giant Facebook shows that billions of consumers are still seemingly in blissful ignorance of their role in the whole scheme.

Media and privacy experts have been pointing out for years that, with a free service you are the product, we are all still wondering when the majority will start caring.

Nothing in life is free. Facebook's free service to consumers is a fallacy. The social media giant's customers are advertisers, some of the world's biggest and smallest brands. In return for keeping up to date with friends, many of whom you wouldn't bother saying hello to on the street, Facebook takes everything about you to maximise how it sells you to advertisers.

Facebook chief executive Mark Zuckerberg took nearly four days to respond to a new wave of news stories and scrutiny, the company likely thinking Facebook could ride this out and the news cycle would move on. After all, scandals and outrage happen on a near daily basis and Facebook was able to ride out the first Cambridge Analytica scandal, reported by then-Guardian journalist Harry Davies in 2015.

The golden rules in crisis management are act quickly, front up even if you don't know exactly what's going on, and it has to be the boss. Facebook badly misread the situation.

Even now, Facebook has attempted to pass the buck down onto Cambridge researcher Aleksandr Kogan, although admitting it "made mistakes". An understatement if ever there was one.

An advertiser wanting to reach certain subsets of consumers is nothing new. But, the value exchange between us and media owner has never been as uneven as it is with Facebook. Never has any media company taken so much and given so little in return.

Television, radio and newspapers have lived off advertising for decades. But, in return they entertain and inform consumers, the information they were able to collect from us was very limited by comparison, largely based on demographics. As business models have changed in the age of the internet, traditional media companies are using more data to understand what their audience likes and what ads they can serve that are more relevant to them, but there is a realisation viewer, reader and listener trust and privacy is paramount.

The breadth and depth of what Facebook is harvesting from consumers is near unprecedented. An easily found scan of your Facebook profile archive is a scary look into what the social network knows about you.

We as the public are complicit. We willingly shared, liked and expressed a huge range of emotions in the quest for a dopamine hit which comes from a new notification. The question is whether it was implicit that we were giving up so much of ourselves in the process or we were deceived.

"The short-term, dopamine-driven feedback loops we've created are destroying how society works," former Facebook executive Chamath Palihapitiya told an audience at Stanford University last year.

"No civil discourse, no co-operation; misinformation, mistruth. And it's not an American problem - this is not about Russians ads. This is a global problem."

Should we delete Facebook? The platform has become so ingrained with how we function socially - it is hard. We are sharing less and less, we've become partly aware of the problem, but friends' birthdays, baby showers, engagement parties, dinners with friends, sports teams and school notifications are all run through Facebook.

Advertising plays an important role in our society, it allows for the creation of amazing content, can be genuinely entertaining and inform smart purchases. But, there is a limit, and Facebook has too often acted in manner where it dismissed or swept under the rug vital matters and criticism. Trust is earned, not given, and Facebook has given us too many reasons not to trust it.

HEADLINE: Ten moves to secure BBL; rights bid due by Easter
TEXT:
Network Ten, backed by its new US owner CBS, is expected to bid aggressively to retain rights to the Big Bash League as Cricket Australia calls for bids for its broadcast deal by Easter.

Cricket Australia's long-awaited tender for its next set of broadcast rights was sent out to interested parties last week and in a surprise move the sport's governing body has asked for bids to be lodged in two weeks.

Sources said Ten will fight to retain the Twenty20 Big Bash League and could potentially lob a bid between $40 million and $60 million a year.

Cricket Australia's tender document is understood to outline it wants a significant free-to-air component for the BBL.

Ten, which paid $20 million a year under the previous deal, has been key to the competition's success. In 2013, Ten secured the rights, taking the BBL onto free-to-air TV for the first time. It had previously been on Fox Sports.

Ten will face much more competition for the BBL than it did during the last rights negotiations. Nine and News Corp, via its subscription channel Fox Sports, have been discussing a joint bid for Cricket Australia's broadcast rights worth between $130 million and $150 million, including taking on the BBL, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review in February.

Optus' interest in broadening its cricket rights is waning and sources said the telco was more concentrated on a new deal for the English Premier League, where its rights run out at the end of next season.

Sources said Cricket Australia would factor in its partnership with Ten, which has seen the Twenty20 tournament grow from an afterthought in the last rights deal to one of the prime pieces of the upcoming contract.

It is understood Ten has retained KordaMentha in an advisory capacity for a number projects at the metropolitan broadcaster. KordaMentha acted as administrator to Ten last year before its sale to CBS and had been advising the network before that. Sources said KordaMentha was not specifically retained to help negotiate cricket rights, rather its role is broader, but it is playing a role. Ten, KordaMentha and Cricket Australia declined to comment.

Source said CBS was acutely aware of the importance of BBL to Ten.

The US broadcaster is a major player in US sports rights, having been part of a $US27.9 billion deal, along with Fox and NBC, for rights to the NFL. It is paying around $US1 billion annually for rights to the American Football Conference.

Cricket Australia is aiming to expand the competition to about 60 games. The 2017-18 season had 43 men's games, with the prospect of extending the competition into February and even March. Industry sources have complained too much cricket on TV during a short period of time has diluted the product, but spreading BBL over a longer period could be better for ratings and advertising dollars.

Sources said Cricket Australia was looking for a deal around $150 million a year, up from $100 million under the old deal, in order to have enough revenue for the sport and deliver on promises made in the collective bargaining agreement it made with its players last year.
